  • HK$1,000,000 became HK$529,252 over 6.0 years, against HK$599,437 for the benchmark — -7.02 pp of cumulative active return, or -1.89 pp a year.
  • Risk-adjusted returns are marginally better than the benchmark (Sharpe -0.07 vs -0.08), but both are negative. The portfolio ran at 40.22% volatility versus 34.41%, and its maximum drawdown was -75.33% against -74.54%.
  • The equity high was 17 Feb 2021 (HK$1,410,364). It then fell 75.33% to 22 Jan 2024 and never regained that high, finishing 62.47% below it.
  • Beta was 1.08 with R² of 0.85, so roughly 85% of monthly variance is explained by the index. Alpha was +0.14% a year with a t-statistic of 0.02 (p = 0.98): indistinguishable from zero.
  • Attribution is lopsided. Tencent contributed -1.50 pp; Alibaba contributed -16.46 pp. Measured by risk, the largest and smallest risk contributions differed by 8 pp despite identical 25% weights.
  • Monthly rebalancing was worth +2.87 pp against simply holding the initial weights, and it lowered volatility from 44.45% to 40.22%. At 10 bps a side the discipline cost 0.03% a year of CAGR, so the gain is not an artefact of transaction costs.
Reading this report. The basket was assembled with the benefit of hindsight and covers one specific stretch for Hong Kong equities. The numbers describe what this specific portfolio did; they are not evidence that equal-weighting these 4 names, or any 4 names, earns a premium. Gross returns are shown throughout, with rebalancing costs isolated in section 08.

Month to date (30 Sep 2026 to 26 Oct 2026, 16 sessions): the portfolio is -4.97% and the benchmark -9.35%. The current month is excluded from every statistic above so that all observations are complete months.

03   Risk

Annualised volatility of 40.22% and a -75.33% peak-to-trough decline define this portfolio more than its return does. The drawdown is not a brief episode: the curve stayed underwater for up to 5.6 years, and the monthly loss distribution has excess kurtosis of 2.05.

Drawdown from running peak (underwater curve), daily. 100% of the initial capital is treated as the high-water mark.

Drawdown history

Drawdowns are separated using a 10% zig-zag rule, so a long bear market is shown as its individual legs rather than one six-year episode. The deepest single leg was -45.24% in 33 days (10 Feb 2022 to 15 Mar 2022); the cumulative peak-to-trough decline from the 17 Feb 2021 high to the 22 Jan 2024 low was -75.33%. 04   Benchmark comparison

The portfolio is a higher-beta expression of the same theme rather than a diversifier: beta 1.08, R² 0.85, tracking error 15.83%. Concentration in 4 names produced 102% up-capture and 103% down-capture against the index.

Each point is one month. The line is the OLS fit; the intercept is alpha (annualised in the table).

Regression and relative statistics

Alpha is the annualised intercept of a regression of monthly portfolio returns on monthly benchmark returns, with Newey–West standard errors to account for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. Up- and down-capture are the average portfolio return in benchmark up and down months, divided by the benchmark's average in those months.

07   Rolling behaviour

Rolling windows show whether the risk profile was stable or episodic. A portfolio that holds its beta and volatility over time can be assessed on average statistics; one whose risk moves with the cycle cannot.

Twelve-month rolling windows, monthly data. Rolling beta is measured against the benchmark; the dashed line marks beta = 1.

What the rolling windows show

  • Rolling 12-month return ranged from -55.00% to 88.84%; the benchmark ranged from -55.24% to 61.91%.
  • The portfolio beat the benchmark in 48% of rolling 12-month windows, and the gap was widest at +29.57% (Nov 2024) and -34.40% (Aug 2025).
  • Rolling beta stayed between 0.85 and 1.31, averaging 1.09 — a higher-beta way to own the same theme, so it amplified the benchmark's moves in both directions.
  • Rolling volatility was higher than the benchmark's in 98% of windows, so the extra risk was not a temporary feature of one episode.

The two estimates differ because monthly sampling discards within-month information and because Hong Kong equities exhibit short-horizon bid–ask and microstructure noise that inflates daily volatility. With 72 monthly observations the sampling error on annualised volatility is roughly ±8% relative, so the gap is within normal tolerance rather than a data error.

09   Appendix

Methodology

Universe. Four Hong Kong-listed stocks, 25% each at inception. Benchmark. Hang Seng Tech Index ETF (3032.HK), buy-and-hold. Rebalancing. At each monthly close, either through trading or by construction, the weights are reset to target. Between rebalances the weights drift with prices, so the reported monthly return is a true buy-and-hold return for that month.

Returns. Adjusted close, so dividends are reinvested and returns are total returns. Monthly returns are compounded from daily returns, not sampled from month-end prices. Inception. The first month-end on which all 5 series have a price (30 Sep 2020); the partial first calendar month is excluded so every observation is a complete month.

Statistics. Volatility is the sample standard deviation of monthly returns times √12. Sharpe and Sortino use annualised arithmetic mean excess return over annualised volatility and downside deviation, with a zero risk-free rate. Alpha and beta are OLS on monthly returns with Newey–West (HAC) standard errors. M² rescales the portfolio Sharpe ratio by benchmark volatility.

Attribution. Return contributions are daily weight-times-return terms, each linked forward at the cumulative growth rate, so they sum exactly to the cumulative return. Risk contributions are marginal contributions to variance from the monthly covariance matrix and sum to 100%.

Assumptions and limitations

  • Risk-free rate. A zero risk-free rate is the base case. If cash yields were materially positive over the window, Sharpe and Sortino are flattered relative to a cash-based calculation; ranking against the benchmark is unaffected because both series share the assumption.
  • Ex-post selection. The four names were chosen knowing how the period turned out, and they are not a random sample of Hong Kong equities. The report describes what this basket did, not what a repeatable strategy would have earned.
  • One regime. 6.0 years covering a single market cycle. Results are conditional on that sequence.
  • Execution frictions. No taxes, bid–ask spread, market impact, lot-size rounding or dividend withholding tax is modelled. The cost table brackets the rebalancing component only, not round-trip costs on the initial purchase.
  • Benchmark total return. The vendor history records no distributions for the benchmark over this window. If the fund distributed and the series does not capture it, the benchmark's total return here is understated and every active-return figure is correspondingly overstated.
  • Sampling noise. With 72 monthly observations, annualised volatility carries a wide relative standard error and Sharpe ratios are correspondingly imprecise. Differences of a few tenths in Sharpe are not meaningful.
  • Survivorship and corporate actions. All four companies remain listed; a basket formed at inception could have included names that did not survive. Vendor-adjusted prices may be revised after splits and special dividends.
